newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico monetary base to boom but seen within range.
newsitem.headline: Mexico monetary base to boom but seen within range.

text.p: Mexico's monetary base is expected to spike up sharply between now and the end of the year, but analysts said the increase will be tied to seasonal demand and not by itself reflect an easing of monetary policy.

Year-end demand will push the monetary base up sharply, but the government is within the signposts for growth of the money supply -- the next one coming up at the end of September. They add that, within the overall perimeters set for growth in the monetary base -- mainly notes and coins -- the central bank has begun to allow for lower interest rates.

"They (the central bank) definitely are on track and they may be even better than originally expected. There is no reason to think that they will go off track with their program," said one Mexico City-based economist.
At the start of the year, the central bank forecast an increase of 18.0 billion pesos in the monetary base by the end of 1996 over the figure at the end of 1995.

The monetary base ended 1995 at 66.8 billion pesos, but the central bank also previously forecast 63 billion pesos as its year-end starting point since they said a sharp increase in December last year was not representative.

At the end of last week, the monetary base was about 60.1 billion pesos, while the central bank's forecast for the end of the third quarter was for about 450 million pesos below the 1995 year-end figure. Economists say this latitude allows room for a sharp year-end increase, traditionally tied to greater holiday spending.

Santander Investment said recently that the nominal monetary base will rise 40 percent from current levels during the fourth quarter "however, this would not imply a relaxation of the monetary policy, because the expansion will be caused by a seasonally higher level of expeditures in the economy."
Within that overall envelope for growth in the monetary aggregates, analysts say the central bank recently has been able to allow interest rates to drift lower.
Interest rates have come down as worries over inflation have eased and as the need to spur greater domestic growth increases.

"It is not because the monetary base may go up in December, but I do think the central bank has adopted a policy of supporting somewhat lower levels of interest rates...," said HSBC James Capel economist Gray Newman.

"That distinguishes central bank policy from the earlier part of this year, when they didn't like to admit it, but when they were much more concerned about stability in the peso and providing overall stability and they were willing to let interest rates rise," Newman said.
Santander noted that the Mexican central bank started to ease after the U.S. Federal Reserve left rates unchanged following its August 20 Open Market Committee meeting.

It said this shows monetary authorities are confident about the downward trend in inflation, which will lead to a drop in real rates next year when monetary policy is seen as being even Exports have led most of the growth in the economic recovery, but as the economy moves to an increase in investment spending, it becomes more sensitive to interest rates, analysts said.
